Series::CalcAccessor API Reference¶

Back to Series API Reference

Series::CalcAccessor groups callable differentiation and anchored callable integration. It does not introduce a second derivative tape. The derivative methods delegate to the centralized higher-order reverse transform, while antidiff() builds quadrature from ordinary differentiable Series operations. The root entrypoint and option-binding syntax are described on Series::calc.

Method Index¶

  • antidiff evaluates first or repeated anchored integrals at every receiver value.

  • diff returns a derivative of any non-negative order, either as the full derivative tensor or the elementwise diagonal.

  • grad returns the first derivative of a scalar objective with the input’s shape.

  • hess returns the second derivative of a scalar objective with two input-axis blocks.

  • jac returns the first derivative of an arbitrary output with output axes followed by input axes.

  • options inspects the defaults bound by x.calc(options).

diff and antidiff are also accessors with named methods for stochastic calculus (see Stochastic Calculus below):

  • diff.ito: Itô’s lemma, product and quotient rules, jumps and time dependence.

  • diff.strat: the Stratonovich differential and drift conversion.

  • diff.marcus: the Marcus differential and jump flow.

  • diff.malliavin: the discrete Malliavin derivative and the Skorokhod integral.

  • antidiff.ito: Itô and θ-integrals along a path.

  • antidiff.strat: Stratonovich integrals along a path.

  • antidiff.marcus: the Marcus integral along a path that jumps.

Choosing A Derivative Form¶

Let the receiver have shape X and let fn(x) have shape Y.

Call

Required callback output

Result shape

x.calc.diff(fn, n)

Any differentiable Y

Y + X repeated n times

x.calc({.elementwise=true}).diff(fn, n)

Exactly X

X

x.calc.grad(fn)

Rank-zero scalar

X

x.calc.jac(fn)

Any differentiable Y

Y + X

x.calc.hess(fn)

Rank-zero scalar

X + X

grad, jac, and hess are constrained call forms over the same engine as diff; they are not separate differentiation systems. Their names make the expected geometry explicit and reject incompatible callback outputs early.

Graph And Dependency Contract¶

The callback must build its result from differentiable Series operations. The transform creates a fresh differentiable leaf internally, evaluates the callback, runs reverse mode with graph retention when another derivative order is needed, and returns the requested derivative. The original receiver need not call tracks_slope_() and does not receive a stored sensitivity.

A derivative is only as differentiable as every operation in the callback’s reverse path. Higher-order requests fail when an operation declares that its reverse rule cannot itself be differentiated. With strict_dependency=false, a genuinely disconnected output contributes zero; with strict_dependency=true, disconnection is an error. This distinction prevents an unsupported higher-order path from being silently advertised as a true zero.

Callable Integration¶

For a receiver u, u.calc.antidiff(fn, a) returns one value per endpoint:

F(u) = integral from a to u of fn(t) dt

The receiver may be scalar or higher-rank. Quadrature nodes are appended as a temporary last axis, so the callback must be vectorized and return exactly the node shape it receives. Repeated integration uses the equivalent weighted single-integral formula and optional lower-bound derivatives; it does not nest host loops or repeatedly invoke a scalar integrator.

Because endpoint construction and quadrature are composed from differentiable Series primitives, reverse mode can continue through the returned integral.

Stochastic Calculus¶

The same two accessors carry the calculus of random processes. Three ideas organize it.

  • A differential (x.calc.diff.ito(g, mu, sigma)) takes a function g and the coefficients of a process dX = μ dt + σ dW and returns the coefficients of g(X): the drift and diffusion, and for processes that jump the effect of each jump. Every element of the receiver is an independent point, so one call covers a grid or a batch of independent processes.

  • An integral (w.calc.antidiff.ito(f, t0, t1)) integrates a function of time and path against a sampled path. The receiver is the path.

  • The convention decides what the symbols mean. Itô reads the integrand at the start of each step; Stratonovich reads the average of both ends and obeys the ordinary chain rule; Marcus extends the Stratonovich rule to paths that jump.

Task

Call

Coefficients of g(X), Itô

x.calc.diff.ito(g, mu, sigma)

Coefficients of g(X), ordinary chain rule

x.calc.diff.strat(g, mu, sigma)

Change the convention of a drift

x.calc.diff.strat_drift / ito_drift

Jumps that follow a flow

x.calc.diff.marcus(...)

Derivative with respect to Brownian increments

dw.calc.diff.malliavin(F)

Integral of f(t, W) against a path, Itô

w.calc.antidiff.ito(f, t0, t1)

The same, Stratonovich

w.calc.antidiff.strat(f, t0, t1)

The same, for an integrand already sampled

f.antidiff(w).ito()

Quadratic variation and covariation

w.antidiff().quadratic_variation()

Simulating stochastic differential equations, checking that an integrand is adapted and diagnosing a path that is not a standard Wiener path belong to the numerical methods library; it forwards to the methods on these pages.

Bound Options¶

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;
options.lower = 0.0;
options.initial = {2.0, 3.0};

auto configured = x.calc(options);
auto derivative = configured.diff(fn);       // order 2
auto integral = configured.antidiff(fn);     // lower 0, order 2

An explicit terminal argument wins over the corresponding bound field: configured.diff(fn, 1) uses order one, and configured.antidiff(fn, -1.0) uses lower bound -1.0. See options for every field and its scope.
